props.title: Themroc
props.initialSlug: Man rejects society, becomes urban cave-dwelling savage

sections.content: **Themroc** (1973) stands as one of cinema's most radical experiments in anarchist filmmaking. Director Claude Faraldo crafted this dialogue-free descent into primitive rebellion using only grunts, screams, and invented language. The film follows a factory worker (Michel Piccoli) who breaks from society, tears down his apartment walls, and creates a cave-dwelling commune. It shares DNA with other European counter-culture provocations like **Weekend** (1967) and **Sweet Movie** (1974), but pushes further into primal territory. The film's influence echoes in later anti-establishment works like **Brazil** (1985) and **Dogtooth** (2009).

sections.content: The 1970s marked a peak for European art-house provocations that attacked social institutions. While **WR: Mysteries of the Organism** (1971) used sexuality as revolution and **The Holy Mountain** (1973) embraced psychedelic spirituality, Themroc stripped away all pretense to expose civilization as a thin veneer over our animal nature. Its influence can be traced through later works about societal dropouts like **Bad Boy Bubby** (1993) and **Survive Style 5+** (2004).

The film's wordless approach connects it to early silent anarchist cinema like **Ménilmontant** (1926), while its critique of modern labor and urban living predicts later works like **Tetsuo: The Iron Man** (1989) and **Delicatessen** (1991). Piccoli's transformation from factory worker to cave-dwelling primitive became a blueprint for characters rejecting society's structures in films like **How to Get Ahead in Advertising** (1989) and **Falling Down** (1993). movies.title: Possession
movies.slug: Intense psychological horror about societal breakdown and personal disintegration

sections.content: While rarely seen today, Themroc's DNA lives on in films that critique capitalism through surreal transformation. **Sorry to Bother You** (2018) shares its workplace rebellion theme, while **Taxidermia** (2006) mirrors its body horror approach to consumption and excess. The film's influence on French extreme cinema can be seen in works like **Trouble Every Day** (2001) and **In My Skin** (2002), which similarly explore primal urges breaking through social conditioning.
